alignment.note: Greek expresses the genitive with article plus noun (τοῦ εὐαγγελίου), whereas Syriac fuses the genitive proclitic ܕ- onto ܐܘܢܓܠܝܘܢ as a single orthographic token; both render the loan-word εὐαγγέλιον, which Latin likewise transliterates as Evangelii. The divergence is purely morphosyntactic in how the genitive is marked.

Greek anarthrous υἱοῦ and Latin Filii leave the possessive unexpressed, while the Peshitta ܒܪܗ carries the pronominal suffix -eh ('his Son'), an explicit anaphoric marker referring back to God; this is a typical Syriac construct-state strategy rather than a substantive theological variant.

Greek marks the genitive of θεός with the article (τοῦ θεοῦ), a reading attested in NA28 though omitted by some witnesses (e.g. ℵ*, Θ); Syriac ܕܐܠܗܐ again prefixes the genitive proclitic ܕ-, and Latin Dei marks the genitive purely by inflection without an article. All three converge on 'of God.'
